title: UFO Moviez and DCDC Partner to Bring Indian Cinema to 33,000 North American Screens
excerpt: India's largest cinema distribution network teams up with North America's leading digital delivery coalition, opening a direct pipeline for Indian films to reach US and Canadian theaters at scale.
body:
• UFO Moviez India and the Digital Cinema Distribution Coalition (DCDC) have partnered to distribute Indian films across North America through DCDC's network of 3,100+ sites and 33,000+ screens.
  • The collaboration begins with the upcoming release of 'The Indian Story,' following the successful North American run of 'Bandar' earlier this year.
  • DCDC's digital delivery infrastructure will streamline how Indian films reach US and Canadian theaters, reducing logistical barriers that have historically limited wide releases.
  • The partnership directly addresses growing demand among North American audiences — including the Indian diaspora — for diverse theatrical content.

A Distribution Pipeline for Indian Cinema

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RSaZod3YiAM

UFO Moviez India Limited and the Digital Cinema Distribution Coalition (DCDC) announced a strategic partnership on August 7 to bring Indian feature films to theaters across North America. The deal connects UFO Moviez's relationships with Indian content owners to DCDC's digital delivery network, which spans more than 3,100 sites and 33,000 screens across the United States and Canada.

The partnership is designed to tackle a persistent bottleneck: getting Indian films onto North American screens at scale. While Bollywood and regional Indian cinema have devoted diaspora audiences in cities like New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Toronto, distribution has traditionally been fragmented, limited to a handful of screens in metro areas with large South Asian populations.

"DCDC's network offers unmatched quality and reach, making it an ideal partner for connecting Indian filmmakers with a broader exhibitor base. There is a tremendous opportunity to grow audiences for Indian cinema throughout North America."

— Rajesh Mishra, Group CEO, UFO Moviez

How the Partnership Works

UFO Moviez operates India's largest cinema technology network, built on a satellite-based digital distribution platform that has delivered more than 11,000 films in 22 languages across Indian theaters. DCDC, meanwhile, is the leading digital cinema delivery service in North America, providing secure, high-speed distribution of feature films, trailers, and alternative content to exhibitors nationwide.

The combination means Indian distributors and filmmakers gain access to a turnkey delivery pipeline. Instead of negotiating individual deals with theater chains or relying on physical media, content can be pushed digitally through DCDC's existing infrastructure — the same network used by Hollywood studios for major releases.

Howard Kiedaisch, CEO of DCDC, noted the increasing appetite among American audiences for international content. "Indian cinema continues to captivate viewers with compelling stories," he said. "This partnership aims to help more of these films reach wider audiences through efficient digital distribution channels."

What It Means for Diaspora Moviegoers

For the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans and millions more across Canada, the partnership could significantly expand where and how they watch Indian films theatrically. The current landscape often requires driving to specific theaters in ethnic enclaves or waiting for streaming releases. Access to 33,000 screens means Indian films could, in theory, play alongside mainstream releases in suburban multiplexes — not just in Edison, New Jersey, or Artesia, California.

The collaboration kicks off with the release of 'The Indian Story,' following the successful North American run of 'Bandar,' which served as a proof-of-concept for the distribution model. UFO Moviez and DCDC plan to use that initial success to broaden the range of Indian films available to North American audiences.

A Growing Market

The timing aligns with a broader trend. Indian films have posted increasingly strong international box office numbers in recent years, driven by blockbusters that transcend language barriers and a diaspora audience willing to pay premium prices for opening-weekend tickets. The challenge has been less about demand and more about supply — specifically, the logistics of getting films onto enough screens quickly enough to capitalize on release-weekend buzz.

With DCDC's infrastructure handling the digital delivery side, UFO Moviez can focus on aggregating content and marketing. The companies have signaled they intend to expand the range of Indian films available over time, covering not just Hindi-language releases but also Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, and other regional cinema — genres that have shown strong international performance in recent years.
